name: Liam Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Liam, thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a dozer at a bauxite mine, open pit, and I lead the dozer and grader crew on my shift, five of us. We strip the topsoil and the overburden, push up the ramps, keep the haul roads graded so the trucks don't shake themselves to bits. I'm on the D10, that's the big one, and I can cut a road to within a couple of centimetres by feel. My grandad worked the old mine on the other side of the hill, my dad did thirty years here, so it's in the blood.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that you can see what you did at the end of the day, a clean bench, a good road. What wears me out is the new rules every month and the fatigue cameras in the cab watching your eyelids. Outside work, there's church on Sunday and the brass band on Thursday, I play the tenor horn. I'm marrying Hannah next autumn, she's a receptionist at the dentist on Mill Road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. That's what I'd guess anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, at the pub and in the band room. Every few years there's some big thing that's supposed to change everything. I'd probably share a joke about it on the band's group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be relieved. I don't use any of it and I don't trust it. If it stays a tool for office people, my dozer's still my dozer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing changes. Keep working, keep saving for the wedding, we've got about three months of bills plus the wedding pot. Book the church and the hall like we planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a Sunday afternoon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you see any automation on your site already?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a remote-control dozer they bring out for the dangerous slopes, run from a box on a guy's chest. Fair enough for the edges where it might roll. But for normal work, no, it can't feel the ground like a man in the seat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would bother you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The cameras and the rules, still. That's not AI, that's head office in the city who's never sat in a cab. But that's been going on since my dad's time, it's not new.

S0.say: I told you so. Every few years there's some big thing that's supposed to change everything, and it doesn't.
S0.think: I'd be relieved, because I don't use it and I don't trust it. If it stays a tool for office people, my dozer's still my dozer.
S0.do: Keeps working and saving for the wedding, with about three months of bills plus a wedding fund. Books the church and the hall as planned.
S0.quote: It can't feel the ground like a man in the seat.
S0.fieldNote: Liam frames his job as family inheritance, three generations at the same hill. He's dismissive of AI and accepts remote dozers only for dangerous slopes. His real irritation is with head office rules and cab cameras, which he sees as an old problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hm. That's closer to what people at work talk about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people should keep working and not panic, and the company owes its loyal workers first go at any new jobs. I'd say it at the pub. I wouldn't post much, I don't like arguing with strangers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it worries me. If they can run one dozer remote on the slopes, they can run five from a room in the city, and that's my crew. And I don't want to sit in a room with a screen, I'd rather drive a tractor for my uncle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going on the dozer and wait to see what the company does. I wouldn't sign up for the remote course unless they made me. We'd still have the wedding but maybe trim the guest list a bit. I'd ask my uncle about his farm, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Sitting in my gut, like a stone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd only do the remote course if they made you. What's behind that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Partly pride, I'll admit it. I'm the best dozer man on the site, and on a screen I'd be a beginner again with twenty-year-olds who play video games. And partly that I just don't trust it. I've seen the remote unit lose signal and sit there like a dead cow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if your crew got cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The people in the city making the decisions, mostly. Not the company on the ground, our managers are local, some went to school with my dad. And not the workers. If it's done fair, with the older men retiring and nobody pushed out, I can live with that.

S1.say: People should keep working and not panic, and the company owes its loyal workers first go at the new jobs. I'd say it at the pub, not online.
S1.think: If they can run one dozer remotely on the slopes, they can run five from a room in the city, and that's my crew. I'd rather drive a tractor for my uncle than sit in a room with a screen.
S1.do: Keeps working on the dozer and waits to see what the company does, refusing the remote course unless required. Trims the wedding guest list a little and asks his uncle about work on the farm, just in case.
S1.feel: Anxious, a stone in his gut.
S1.quote: I've seen the remote unit lose signal and sit there like a dead cow.
S1.fieldNote: Liam's resistance is part pride and part distrust of the technology, and he admits both. He blames distant city decision-makers, not local managers. A fair process, with older men retiring first, is something he says he could accept.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's before the wedding's paid off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is wrong and someone needs to stop it. People need work, not cheques in the post. I'd say it at church and at the pub, and probably to the local paper if they asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd feel like the floor's gone. Three generations on that hill and I'm the one who turns the lights off. Everything I'm good at, a machine does better and doesn't need a lunch break.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First week, I'd sit down with Hannah and her parents and talk about the wedding, maybe do it smaller and sooner. We'd cut everything else, no new truck, no holiday. I'd talk to the pastor and my dad about what we do as a family, maybe go back to my parents' place and save rent. I'd ask my uncle about the farm, but if robots do farming too, I don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicked, honestly. Like the dozer sliding on a wet slope and the brakes not catching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people need work, not cheques. If there were no work, would you take the cheque?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have to, I suppose. I'd hate it. My dad would hate it more. A man's supposed to provide, and if the government's providing, I don't know what I'm for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years of warning give you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. Time to get married, maybe. Time to say goodbye to the crew properly. That's it. I wouldn't know what to train for, and I'm not good at starting over.

S2.say: This is wrong and someone needs to stop it. People need work, not cheques in the post, and I would say that at church and at the pub.
S2.think: I'd feel like the floor's gone, three generations on that hill and I'm the one who turns the lights off. Everything I'm good at, a machine does better and doesn't need a lunch break.
S2.do: Talks with Hannah and her parents about a smaller, sooner wedding and cuts all other spending. Leans on his pastor and family, considers moving back in with his parents to save rent, and asks his uncle about farm work.
S2.feel: Panicked, like a dozer sliding on a wet slope with the brakes not catching.
S2.quote: Three generations on that hill and I'm the one who turns the lights off.
S2.fieldNote: This scenario hits Liam's sense of who he is, not just his income. He'd accept government support only reluctantly, because providing for his family is central to him. He sees two years as time to marry and say goodbye, not to adapt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. A bit more room. Not much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should be training young people for real trades now, apprenticeships, not just handing out money later. I'd say it at the band and to anyone standing for council. And I'd say the companies owe the towns that built them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd get maybe three or four more years on the dozer. Then I'd be thirty-one with a wife, maybe a baby, and no trade a robot can't do. I'd be scared, but I wouldn't show it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd still marry next autumn as planned. I'd save harder, no new truck, aim for eight months of bills. I'd vote for whoever promises to keep people working, even if it slows things down. I wouldn't retrain, not unless I could see something solid at the end of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake on Sunday nights before the week starts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said maybe a baby. Would this change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably still try. Hannah wants kids young, so do I. My mum had me at twenty-four in a bad year for the mine, and we got by with the garden and the church. But I'd be more scared than my parents were.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from your church or community?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just what they already do, but more. The meals roster, the men's breakfast, people looking out for each other. If the work goes, that's what's left. I'd want to help run it, actually, it'd give me something to do.

S3.say: We should be training young people for real trades now, with apprenticeships, not just handing out money later. The companies owe the towns that built them.
S3.think: I'd get maybe three or four more years on the dozer, then be thirty-one with a wife, maybe a baby, and no trade a robot can't do. I'd be scared, but I wouldn't show it.
S3.do: Marries next autumn as planned, skips the new truck and aims for eight months of savings. Votes for whoever promises to keep people working and won't retrain unless something solid lies at the end.
S3.feel: Alarmed, lying awake on Sunday nights before the week starts.
S3.quote: I'd be scared, but I wouldn't show it.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets Liam keep his wedding plan but not his confidence. He wants work and apprenticeships, not handouts, and would vote to slow the change. He sees church and community support as what would remain, and would want a role in running it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. Kids at school, probably.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do it properly, slowly, without ruining towns. Keep people working as long as possible and phase it in. I'd say that to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it'd sit on me the whole ten years. I'd be on the dozer most of that time, but I'd know. It's like knowing your dad's sick, every good day has that underneath.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, nothing big. Keep working, keep saving, go ahead with the wedding and maybe a house in a few years. I'd go to the council meetings and push for apprenticeships in things that last. I wouldn't change jobs until I had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, but slow. A low hum, not a siren.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said like knowing your dad's sick. Can you say more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad had a heart scare two years ago, he's fine now. But for a while, every barbecue felt like a countdown. Ten years of warning would be like that. You still enjoy it, but you're always counting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the difference between two years and ten, for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten, I can marry, have a kid, maybe pay a bit off the house. With two, I'm just bracing. But in both, the end's the same, and I don't have a plan for the end. I don't think ten years would give me one, honestly, I'm not built that way.

S4.say: Ten years is enough time to do it properly and slowly, without ruining towns. Keep people working as long as possible and phase it in.
S4.think: It would sit on me for the whole ten years, like knowing your dad's sick. I'd be on the dozer most of that time, but every good day would have that underneath.
S4.do: Keeps working and saving through year one, goes ahead with the wedding and plans a house in a few years. Attends council meetings to push for apprenticeships in lasting trades and stays in his job until forced to move.
S4.feel: Alarmed, but slowly, like a low hum rather than a siren.
S4.quote: You still enjoy it, but you're always counting.
S4.fieldNote: For Liam, more time softens the shock but not the worry, because he doesn't expect to find a plan for the end point. His father's heart scare shapes how he imagines ten years of warning. He'd use the time for family milestones and local politics, not for changing careers.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. It doesn't give me time to marry Hannah properly or say goodbye to the crew. What would help is the company and the government keeping people in real jobs as long as possible, apprenticeships for the young ones, and help that comes through the community, not just a cheque from far away.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask what work means to people. For me it's not just money, it's being useful, being the one who can do the hard thing. If you take that away, a cheque won't fix it. The church helps, but it's not the same as a bench you cut yourself.

headlineQuote: A man's supposed to provide, and if the government's providing, I don't know what I'm for.
portrait: Liam Schmidt is 27 and leads the dozer and grader crew at an open-pit bauxite mine, the third generation of his family to work the same hill. He plays tenor horn in the brass band, goes to church on Sundays and is marrying Hannah next autumn. He avoids new technology, never uses AI, and distrusts remote machines that lose signal. Through the scenarios his worry deepens fast: anxious with steady change, panicked with two years, and alarmed even with ten. He wants work and apprenticeships rather than handouts, blames distant city decision-makers, and leans on family, church and community.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because it leaves no time to marry Hannah properly or say goodbye to his crew.
whatWouldHelp: Keeping people in real jobs as long as possible, apprenticeships for young people, and help that comes through the community rather than a cheque from far away.
